en.title: Verbs followed by infinitive or gerund
en.summary: Some verbs take the infinitive, some the gerund, and a few change meaning.

paragraphs: After a verb, English uses either the to-infinitive or the -ing form, and the choice depends on the first verb. You have to learn which verbs take which form. A few verbs can take either, with the same or a different meaning.

blocks.html:
InfinitiveGerund
want, hope, plan, decide, promise, refuse, manage, affordenjoy, finish, avoid, consider, suggest, mind, keep, practise
I decided to leave.I finished working.
She refused to go.He suggested going.

sections.title: Either form with the same meaning

paragraphs: Like, love, hate, prefer, begin, start and continue can take either form with little difference in meaning. The infinitive is slightly more usual for a particular occasion, and the gerund for a general activity.

blocks.html:
General (gerund)Particular (infinitive)
I like swimming.I'd like to swim today.
She loves dancing.She'd love to dance.

Verb+ infinitive+ gerund
rememberRemember to lock the door. (do it)I remember locking it. (I did it)
forgetDon't forget to call.I'll never forget meeting her.
stopHe stopped to rest. (in order to)He stopped working. (ended it)
tryTry to be quiet. (make an effort)Try adding salt. (experiment)
regretI regret to say... (sad news)I regret saying that. (past action)

items: Wrong: **I enjoy to swim.** Right: **I enjoy swimming.**
Wrong: **I want swimming.** Right: **I want to swim.**
Wrong: **She stopped to smoke.** (if you mean she quit) Right: **stopped smoking**
